content: In a previously healthy 7-month-old child, the disease progressed rapidly to severe systemic illness despite hospitalization. Clinical manifestations included microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with renal involvement, coagulopathy, and hyponatremia. Fortunately, the child recovered, and none of the cutaneous anthrax cases diagnosed after the 2001 attacks were fatal. Gastrointestinal anthrax is thought to occur after the deposition and germination of spores in the upper or lower gastrointestinal tract. However, given the rapid transit time in the gastrointestinal tract, it is more likely that many cases result from the ingestion of large numbers of vegetative bacilli from poorly cooked infected meat rather than from spores. The oral-pharyngeal form of the disease leads to oral or esophageal ulcers, regional lymphadenopathy, edema, and sepsis. Disease in the lower gastrointestinal tract manifests as primary intestinal lesions, predominantly in the terminal ileum or cecum, initially presenting with nausea, vomiting, and malaise, and rapidly progressing to bloody diarrhea, acute abdomen, or sepsis. Massive ascites has been reported in some cases of gastrointestinal anthrax. Advanced infection may resemble the sepsis syndrome seen in inhalational or cutaneous anthrax. Aggressive medical intervention, as recommended for inhalational anthrax, may reduce mortality, but early diagnosis of gastrointestinal anthrax is challenging, and mortality remains high. Postmortem examinations in Sverdlovsk revealed gastrointestinal submucosal lesions in 39 of 42 patients, but all had definitive evidence of inhalational infection. No gastrointestinal anthrax cases were diagnosed in the Sverdlovsk series or following the 2001 anthrax attacks. Determining individual exposure to Bacillus anthracis based on environmental testing is complex due to the uncertain specificity and sensitivity of rapid field tests and the difficulty in assessing individual exposure risks. A patient presenting with acute nonspecific febrile illness and symptoms consistent with anthrax, whose condition rapidly deteriorates, should prompt consideration of anthrax infection. Recognition of cutaneous anthrax cases may also serve as the first evidence of an anthrax attack. Abnormal findings on chest X-ray or CT scan are diagnostically significant. While anthrax does not cause classic bronchopneumonia, it can result in widened mediastinum, massive pleural effusions, air bronchograms, necrotizing pneumonic lesions, and/or consolidation, leading to hypoxemia and imaging abnormalities that may mimic pneumonia. In the 2001 anthrax attacks, all 10 initial patients had abnormal chest X-ray results, and 8 patients with CT scans showed abnormalities, including widened mediastinum and effusions. Such findings in a previously healthy patient with febrile illness or sepsis strongly suggest advanced inhalational anthrax. In advanced inhalational anthrax, the bacterial burden may be so high that bacilli are visible on Gram stain of peripheral blood, as observed in the 2001 attacks. The most useful microbiologic test is a standard blood culture, which typically shows growth within 6 to 24 hours. Blood cultures obtained before antibiotic initiation were positive in all 8 patients tested during the 2001 attacks. However, blood cultures may become sterilized after even one or two doses of antibiotics, emphasizing the importance of obtaining cultures before starting therapy. If the laboratory is alerted to the possibility of anthrax, biochemical testing and review of colonial morphology can provide a preliminary diagnosis within 12 to 24 hours after inoculation. Definitive diagnosis can be confirmed by an LRN (Laboratory Response Network) laboratory. If the clinical laboratory is not alerted, B. anthracis may not be correctly identified, as routine procedures often identify Bacillus species without further specification unless specifically requested. This is because Bacillus species are often dismissed as contaminants, such as Bacillus cereus. Given the potential for future anthrax attacks, routine clinical laboratory procedures should be modified to specifically exclude B. anthracis when Bacillus species bacteremia is identified, unless compelling reasons suggest otherwise. If exclusion is not possible, the isolate should be transferred to an LRN laboratory. Sputum culture and Gram stain are unlikely to be diagnostic for inhalational anthrax due to the frequent absence of a pneumonic process. In the 2001 series, Gram stain of sputum was positive in only one case of inhalational anthrax. For suspected cutaneous anthrax, Gram stain and culture of vesicular fluid should be performed. If Gram stain is negative or the patient is already on antibiotics, a punch biopsy should be conducted, and specimens sent to a laboratory capable of immunohistochemical staining or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays. Blood cultures should also be obtained, and antibiotics initiated pending confirmation of inhalational or cutaneous anthrax diagnosis. Nasal swabs were used in some individuals believed to be at risk of inhalational anthrax following the 2001 attacks. While studies have shown the presence of B. anthracis spores in the nares of monkeys after experimental exposure, the predictive value of nasal swabs for diagnosing inhalational anthrax in humans is unknown and untested. It is also unclear how quickly antibiotics render spore recovery from nasal swabs impossible. One patient who died from inhalational anthrax had a negative nasal swab. Consequently, the CDC advised in 2001 that nasal swabs should not be used as a clinical diagnostic test. If obtained for epidemiological purposes, nasal swab results should not be used to rule out infection in a patient. Individuals with positive nasal swab results for B. anthracis should receive postexposure antibiotic prophylaxis, as a positive swab indicates exposure to aerosolized B. anthracis. Antibodies to the protective antigen (PA) of B. anthracis, termed anti-PA IgG, have been shown to confer immunity in animal models following anthrax vaccination.
